title: Theory of Computation True or False Quiz
description: True/False practice questions covering Finite Automata, Context Free Grammars, Turing Machines, and Complexity Classes.
heading: Theory of Computation True or False

questions.question: Every NDFA can be converted into an equivalent DFA.
questions.explanation: True: The subset construction algorithm guarantees that any non-deterministic finite automaton can be simulated by an equivalent deterministic finite automaton.

questions.question: A string is a set of symbols taken from an alphabet.
questions.explanation: False: A string is an ordered finite sequence of symbols, not an unordered set.

questions.question: DFA may have multiple transitions for the same input symbol from a state.
questions.explanation: False: By definition, a Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) has exactly one unique transition out of a state for each input symbol.

questions.question: Moore and Mealy machines are equivalent in computational power.
questions.explanation: True: Any Mealy machine can be converted into an equivalent Moore machine and vice versa, meaning they accept or generate matching regular language translations.

questions.question: Pumping Lemma is used to prove that a language is regular.
questions.explanation: False: The Pumping Lemma is a negative test used via contradiction to prove a language is non-regular; it cannot prove a language is regular.

questions.question: A derivation tree represents the structure of a string in CFG.
questions.explanation: True: A derivation tree (or parse tree) graphically presents the hierarchical grammatical structure of a valid string derived from a Context-Free Grammar.

questions.question: A grammar is ambiguous if a string has more than one parse tree.
questions.explanation: True: Structural ambiguity is defined by the existence of two or more distinct parse trees (or leftmost/rightmost derivations) for at least one string in the language.

questions.question: Chomsky Normal Form allows productions of the form A → ABC.
questions.explanation: False: Chomsky Normal Form (CNF) strictly limits production configurations to either a single terminal (A → a) or exactly two non-terminals (A → BC).

questions.question: Pushdown Automata use a stack as memory.
questions.explanation: True: A PDA is essentially a finite automaton augmented with an external LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) stack memory structure.

questions.question: Every CFG has an equivalent PDA.
questions.explanation: True: Context-Free Languages are precisely the class of languages recognized by Pushdown Automata, meaning every CFG can be converted into a matching PDA.

questions.question: A Turing Machine has infinite tape.
questions.explanation: True: A Turing Machine features a tape memory structure that is unbounded and extends infinitely, acting as unrestricted workspace memory.

questions.question: The Halting Problem is decidable.
questions.explanation: False: Alan Turing famously proved that the Halting Problem is undecidable; there exists no general algorithm capable of correctly guessing if every arbitrary program stalls or executes indefinitely.

questions.question: Recursive languages are always decidable.
questions.explanation: True: By definition, a language is recursive if and only if there is a corresponding Turing Machine that decides it, meaning it halts and gives a clear answer for all inputs.

questions.question: Recursively enumerable languages are always decidable.
questions.explanation: False: Recursively enumerable languages are only semi-decidable; their corresponding Turing Machine is guaranteed to halt if the string belongs to the language, but it may loop infinitely if it does not.

questions.question: All variants of Turing Machines are equivalent in power.
questions.explanation: True: Variations like multi-tape, non-deterministic, or semi-infinite tape Turing Machines change the design efficiency or ease, but they all accept the exact same class of languages.

questions.question: Class P consists of problems solvable in polynomial time.
questions.explanation: True: The complexity class P contains all decision problems that can be solved efficiently on a deterministic Turing machine within an upper bound of O(n^k) computational steps.

questions.question: NP problems cannot be verified in polynomial time.
questions.explanation: False: The core definition of NP (Nondeterministic Polynomial time) is the group of problems whose solution certificates can be verified quickly in polynomial time by a deterministic machine.

questions.question: Co-NP contains complements of NP problems.
questions.explanation: True: Co-NP is the computational complexity class containing the decision problem complements of the problems in class NP.

questions.question: Intractable problems are always unsolvable.
questions.explanation: False: Intractable problems are solvable, but they cannot be completed efficiently; they require worse-than-polynomial scaling resources (like exponential time) as input size grows.

questions.question: Time complexity measures the amount of memory used by an algorithm.
questions.explanation: False: Time complexity measures the scale of operational execution steps or computation runtime; memory utilization is measured separately by space complexity.

questions.question: Cook’s Theorem proves that SAT is NP-complete.
questions.explanation: True: Cook's Theorem established the Boolean Satisfiability problem (SAT) as the very first NP-complete problem, laying the groundwork for complexity theory.

questions.question: PSPACE includes problems solvable using polynomial space.
questions.explanation: True: PSPACE represents the class of decision problems solvable by a Turing Machine using a total memory storage footprint bounded by a polynomial function of input size.

questions.question: Savitch’s Theorem shows NP = P.
questions.explanation: False: Savitch's Theorem relates deterministic and non-deterministic space boundaries, proving that NSPACE(f(n)) ⊆ SPACE(f(n)^2). It does not resolve the P vs NP time issue.

questions.question: L class consists of problems solvable in logarithmic space.
questions.explanation: True: The complexity class L denotes problems that can be processed using only a highly restricted workspace memory footprint scaling to O(log n).

questions.question: NL is the same as deterministic log-space class.
questions.explanation: False: NL represents Nondeterministic Logarithmic space, which utilizes parallel computational choice steps. Whether L equals NL remains an open question in computer science.
